lead: Some resistor groups have three terminals and no simple series or parallel path. A star joins three resistors at one centre node; a delta joins them as a triangle. At the three outside terminals the two can behave the same. The star-delta transformation swaps one for the other using fixed resistor formulas. It exists so that a bridge or a three-terminal network can be reduced to series and parallel parts. Power supplies, three-phase loads and bridge sensors use the same three-terminal idea.
prereq: You need: series and parallel reduction and the divider rules from 1.5, and KCL/KVL from 1.3.

sections.h3: When three terminals are not series or parallel

blocks.text: A star is three resistors R<sub>A</sub>, R<sub>B</sub>, R<sub>C</sub> joined at one centre node N; their free ends are terminals A, B, C. A delta is three resistors R<sub>AB</sub>, R<sub>BC</sub>, R<sub>CA</sub> joined as a closed triangle between the same three terminals. If the outside circuit touches only A, B, C, the inside is a three-terminal network. Some syllabi call the star a Y or wye and the delta a Δ.

Series and parallel rules fail in a bridge because one resistor sits between two branches. A star or delta inside the bridge blocks the reduction. Replacing that group by its other form removes the block and turns the circuit into series-parallel parts.

The replacement is equivalent at the terminals: the same voltages at A, B, C give the same currents into A, B, C. The internal currents are not the same. Do not use the equivalent star/delta arms to find the power in each individual resistor of the original group; total terminal power is unchanged.

Name the delta resistors R<sub>AB</sub> between A and B, R<sub>BC</sub> between B and C, and R<sub>CA</sub> between C and A. Let S<sub>Δ</sub> = R<sub>AB</sub> + R<sub>BC</sub> + R<sub>CA</sub>. The equivalent star has centre N and arms R<sub>A</sub>, R<sub>B</sub>, R<sub>C</sub>.
R<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>AB</sub> R<sub>CA</sub> / S<sub>Δ</sub>; R<sub>B</sub> = R<sub>AB</sub> R<sub>BC</sub> / S<sub>Δ</sub>; R<sub>C</sub> = R<sub>BC</sub> R<sub>CA</sub> / S<sub>Δ</sub>
blocks.where: All resistors are in Ω. R<sub>A</sub> is the star arm at terminal A. S<sub>Δ</sub> is the sum of the three delta resistors, in Ω.

blocks.text: Look at the terminal letter. R<sub>A</sub> uses the two delta resistors that touch A, namely R<sub>AB</sub> and R<sub>CA</sub>. R<sub>B</sub> uses R<sub>AB</sub> and R<sub>BC</sub>. R<sub>C</sub> uses R<sub>BC</sub> and R<sub>CA</sub>. The denominator is always the full delta sum.

sections.h3: Star to delta and the balanced case

blocks.text: Go the other way with the star arms R<sub>A</sub>, R<sub>B</sub>, R<sub>C</sub>. Let P = R<sub>A</sub>R<sub>B</sub> + R<sub>B</sub>R<sub>C</sub> + R<sub>C</sub>R<sub>A</sub>. The delta resistors are:
R<sub>AB</sub> = P / R<sub>C</sub>; R<sub>BC</sub> = P / R<sub>A</sub>; R<sub>CA</sub> = P / R<sub>B</sub>
blocks.where: P is the sum of the three products of star arms, in Ω². Each result is in Ω. The denominator is the star arm opposite the delta side: R<sub>C</sub> for side AB.

blocks.text: Balanced case: all star arms equal R<sub>Y</sub>, all delta sides equal R<sub>Δ</sub>. Then P = 3R<sub>Y</sub>² and R<sub>Δ</sub> = 3R<sub>Y</sub>. The reverse is R<sub>Y</sub> = R<sub>Δ</sub>/3. Use this as a quick check: 9 Ω star arms give 27 Ω delta sides, and 30 Ω delta sides give 10 Ω star arms.

In a bridge, pick the star or delta whose replacement creates a series or parallel pair. Convert once, redraw, then use series-parallel reduction from 1.5. Do not convert again unless the redrawn circuit still has a three-terminal block.

figure.caption: A star around centre N at terminals A, B, C and a delta with corners P = A, Q = B, R = C. The labels use the worked example values, so the two forms are terminal-equivalent at terminals A, B, C.

spec.aria: A star of three resistors on the left at terminals A, B, C and a delta of three resistors on the right with corners P = A, Q = B, R = C, using the worked example values.

examples.question: A delta has R<sub>AB</sub> = 10 Ω, R<sub>BC</sub> = 20 Ω, R<sub>CA</sub> = 30 Ω. Find the equivalent star resistors.
steps: Sum the delta resistors: S<sub>Δ</sub> = 10 + 20 + 30 = 60 Ω.
R<sub>B</sub> = R<sub>AB</sub> R<sub>BC</sub> / S<sub>Δ</sub> = 10 × 20 / 60 = 200 / 60 = 10/3 Ω = 3.333 Ω.
examples.answer: The equivalent star has R<sub>A</sub> = 5 Ω, R<sub>B</sub> = 3.333 Ω, and R<sub>C</sub> = 10 Ω.
examples.check:
R_AB = 10.0
R_BC = 20.0
R_CA = 30.0
S = R_AB + R_BC + R_CA
R_A = R_AB * R_CA / S
R_B = R_AB * R_BC / S
R_C = R_BC * R_CA / S
print(round(R_A, 3))
print(round(R_B, 3))
print(round(R_C, 3))

traps: Wrong numerator order in delta-to-star: R<sub>A</sub> must use R<sub>AB</sub> and R<sub>CA</sub>, because those are the two delta resistors touching terminal A.
Using the delta sum as the denominator in star-to-delta. There the denominator is one star arm, the arm opposite the delta side being found.

Saying the two networks are the same everywhere. They are equivalent only at the three outside terminals. Internal currents and the power in each individual original resistor can differ. Total power entering the terminals is unchanged.
Reversing the balanced formulas. R<sub>Y</sub> = R<sub>Δ</sub>/3, but R<sub>Δ</sub> = 3R<sub>Y</sub>; the factor 3 is not used both ways.
Mixing units in one formula. Convert all resistances to Ω before adding or dividing, then attach Ω to the answer.

quiz.q: State the delta-to-star formula for R<sub>A</sub>.
Why does a star-delta transformation help in a bridge circuit?
quiz.a: A bridge has a resistor between two branches, so simple series-parallel reduction stops. Replacing a star by a delta, or a delta by a star, removes that block and allows series-parallel reduction.

quiz.q: A balanced delta has R<sub>AB</sub> = R<sub>BC</sub> = R<sub>CA</sub> = 45 Ω. Find each equivalent star resistor.
quiz.a: Balanced delta to star: R<sub>Y</sub> = R<sub>Δ</sub>/3 = 45/3 = 15 Ω. Each star arm is 15 Ω.

quiz.q: A star has R<sub>A</sub> = 6 Ω, R<sub>B</sub> = 3 Ω, R<sub>C</sub> = 2 Ω. Find R<sub>AB</sub>.
quiz.a: P = R<sub>A</sub>R<sub>B</sub> + R<sub>B</sub>R<sub>C</sub> + R<sub>C</sub>R<sub>A</sub> = 6×3 + 3×2 + 2×6 = 18 + 6 + 12 = 36 Ω². R<sub>AB</sub> = P/R<sub>C</sub> = 36/2 = 18 Ω.

quiz.q: In delta-to-star conversion, why does R<sub>A</sub> use R<sub>AB</sub> and R<sub>CA</sub>, not R<sub>AB</sub> and R<sub>BC</sub>?
quiz.a: R<sub>A</sub> is the star arm at terminal A. The delta resistors touching A are R<sub>AB</sub> and R<sub>CA</sub>. R<sub>BC</sub> is opposite A and does not touch A, so it is not in the numerator for R<sub>A</sub>.

quiz.q: A student uses R<sub>A</sub> + R<sub>B</sub> + R<sub>C</sub> as the denominator in star-to-delta. What simple check fails for equal star arms of 9 Ω?
quiz.a: A balanced star of 9 Ω must give delta sides of 3×9 = 27 Ω. The wrong denominator gives 9 Ω, so the balanced relation R<sub>Δ</sub> = 3R<sub>Y</sub> fails.

quiz.q: Write the balanced relations between R<sub>Y</sub> and R<sub>Δ</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same transformation is used in three-phase motor equivalent circuits, where a delta-connected load is converted to an equivalent star for per-phase analysis. It also appears in bridge sensors and in circuit simulators that reduce resistor networks before solving. Search next for 'balanced three-phase equivalent circuit', 'bridge star-delta conversion', and 'resistor network reduction'.
